transcript:
>> This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
>> Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston.
President Trump held a wide-ranging news conference
at the White House yesterday, just hours after returning
from a four-day trip to Asia.
He praised his meetings with Russian President Vladimir Putin
and Chinese leader Xi Jinping before turning to the U.S. economy.
Trump pointed to falling crude oil prices
and suggested the midterm elections had something to do
with the recent drop.
>> Crude oil prices have plummeted right
since the end of the election.
I wonder how that happened.
Crude oil is down 20% since the start of November,
and now it's down to close to $80 a barrel,
and one of the largest drops, they say, in the history of oil.
It's the biggest drop on record.
>> U.S. crude futures settled Friday
at just under $84 a barrel.
That's down about 13% from election day.
There have been much steeper drops,
including a nearly 80% slide in the second half of 2008.
The president also threatened to tax U.S. companies
that build AI data centers overseas.
He says companies that build abroad could face
what he calls a tremendous tax.
Trump says the goal is to help the U.S. compete with China.
A federal judge in Virginia has blocked the president's
triumphal arch from the foreseeable future.
NPR's Rachel Treisman reports this is the second court
to rule against it this week.
>> The Virginia judge is issuing a preliminary injunction
blocking the project indefinitely.
This comes at the request of Arlington County,
which sued in early October.
Judge Leonie Brinkema says the arch is unlikely
to succeed in court
because of the lack of congressional approval
and rushed federal review.
The arch was already under a temporary restraining order
from a federal judge in D.C.,
who this week extended her block on construction
through December 3rd.
But Brinkema's injunction could delay the project much longer.
The Justice Department told NPR
it will appeal her decision immediately.
Rachel Treisman, NPR News.
>> Tech stocks and shares on Wall Street plummeting this week.
NPR's Stephen Besaha reports the Nasdaq composite
wiped out its gains for the year.
>> There was plenty of positive news
from artificial intelligence companies this week.
>> NVIDIA reported earnings
that easily beat Wall Street expectations.
And Enthropic had a record-setting public offering Thursday.
None of that stopped a rough end of the week on the market.
NVIDIA's stock continued its nosedive,
down about 12% for the day.
Enthropic's stock fell close to 10%.
All that signals that investors are expecting an AI slowdown.
When positive signs for Thanksgiving travelers
looking to drive rather than fly next week,
the national average for a gallon of gas
is down to $3.68, according to AAA,
a drop of about 50 cents from the start of November.
Stephen Besaha, NPR News, Birmingham, Alabama.
>> You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
The Justice Department is pushing back on a request
to block the Army from detonating roughly five tons
of an unstable, lead-based explosive in southeast Iowa.
Tom Barton from Iowa Public Radio reports
the Federal Appeals Court has temporarily suspended the permit.
>> The Army moved the blast from Friday to Monday.
They could still go ahead if the court lifts its hold
on the EPA permit.
Two environmental groups say the agency
didn't fully consider safer ways to dispose of the explosive.
Earth Justice Attorney Tien Chiao
says the lead dust could cross state lines.
>> It does truly feel unprecedented, right,
taking this much explosive that contains lead
and to blow it up knowing that it is going to disperse
over communities, over farmland, over water bodies.
>> The Army says handling the drums for chemical treatment
could trigger an accidental explosion.
The court hasn't said when it will rule.
For NPR News, I'm Tom Barton in Des Moines.
>> Rescue crews are navigating flooded streets in Florida
after days of heavy rain along the state's Atlantic coast.
Lieutenant Grant Eller,
with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission,
says crews are trying to help people
who've been forced from their homes.
>> Do whatever we can to help them out,
whether it's get in, get some of their belongings out
so that they'll be stable until they can return to their home
and assess the damage fully,
or even help them go to the local shelter.
>> The rain has eased in central Florida,
but forecasters say the St. Johns River
could keep rising for several more days.
This is NPR News.

topics.text: Trump touts falling oil prices and links midterm elections to the drop
Trump threatens tax on U.S. companies building AI data centers overseas
Virginia judge blocks Trump's triumphal arch indefinitely at Arlington County's request
Tech stocks slide on Wall Street as NVIDIA and Anthropic shares fall
National average gas price falls to $3.68 ahead of Thanksgiving travel
Justice Department appeals court order blocking Army's five-ton explosive detonation in Iowa
Rescue crews navigate flooded streets in Florida after days of heavy rain
